newsitem.title: USA: NASA ends Pioneer 10 mission after 25 years.
newsitem.headline: NASA ends Pioneer 10 mission after 25 years.

text.p: On the edge of the solar system, 6.2 billion miles (9.9 billion kms) from home, mankind's most distant interplanetary explorer transmitted its last breath of science data on Monday as U.S. space agency NASA pulled the plug on its 25-year mission.

The Pioneer 10 probe blasted off from Cape Canaveral on March 2, 1972, carrying along with its instruments a greeting plaque from humanity depicting a naked man and woman, the man's hand raised in a gesture of friendship.

A 230-foot (70-metre) radio dish near Madrid, Spain, captured the probe's final science transmission at about 2:45 p.m. EST (1945 GMT), said Larry Lasher, the project manager. The signal had taken more than nine hours to reach Earth and was a billionth of a trillionth of a watt strong.
For controllers at NASA's Ames Research Centre, in Mountain View, California, who monitored the probe daily, it was an emotional moment.
"Some of them have been on this mission for 20 years and this is their last day," Lasher said. "It was quite traumatic, quite a loss for those people."
Pioneer 10's radioactive power source was ebbing away and NASA decided the scientific return did not justify the expense of operating the spacecraft.

Of its original 11 instruments only one remained operational, and that was expected to be starved of power by the end of the year. A few months later the spacecraft's transmitter will also fall silent.
The probe was the first to penetrate the rocky asteroid belt and visit Jupiter, confirming the massive planet was made up of gas and liquid.
"It paved the way for all future spacecraft to go out there," he said.
Pioneer's useful life is not over, however. Budding spacecraft operators preparing to control NASA's coming Lunar Prospector project will use the spacecraft for training purposes.
The probe's control centre was to be inherited by the lunar mission, which is scheduled for launch in September.

Pioneer 10 was more than a scientific and engineering marvel. It worked its way into popular culture, appearing in several science fiction books and films. The Klingons once used it for target practice in a Star Trek film.
Should the probe ever fall into the hands of extraterrestrials, its gold plaque is also engraved with Earth's location in the galaxy.
It would be more than 30,000 years before the probe comes close to another star, Ross 248, after crossing the void of interstellar space.
